Select columns from a GPU table

Source: R/select.R
select.tbl_gpu.Rd

Keeps only the specified columns from a GPU table, similar to dplyr::select(). Supports tidyselect syntax for flexible column selection.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
select(.data, ...)

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu object created by tbl_gpu().

...

Column names or tidyselect expressions specifying which columns to keep. Supports:

  • Column names: select(x, y, z)

  • Negative selection: select(-x)

  • Range: select(x:z)

  • Predicates: where(is.numeric). Base type tests (is.numeric, is.double, is.integer, is.character, is.logical, is.factor, is.ordered, inherits(x, "Date")), bare or combined in a lambda such as ~ is.numeric(.x) || is.factor(.x), are answered from the column types. Any other predicate (where(~ anyNA(.x)), lubridate::is.Date), and any call that is not a tidyselect helper or a base name builder (sort(names(x)), paste0(), rev(), setdiff(), .data$x, ... with safe arguments), is resolved on the data: a notified CPU fallback that collects the table

  • Helpers: starts_with(), ends_with(), contains(), etc.

  • Renaming while selecting: select(new_name = old_name)

Value

A tbl_gpu object containing only the selected columns. Column order matches the order specified in the selection; any new = old selections are renamed in the result.

Details

Column selection creates a new GPU table with only the selected columns. The original data remains in GPU memory until garbage collected.

Renaming

select(new_name = old_name) both selects and renames old_name. This is schema-only (see rename.tbl_gpu()): the underlying selection still runs as one gpu_select() gather, with the rename applied on top of it as a separate, schema-only ast_rename() step whenever the tidyselect resolution renamed a column.

Grouped tables

Grouping columns that the selection leaves out are added in front, with the message "Adding missing grouping variables", as in dplyr. Groups follow their column by position, so select(group_by(df, a), a = b) is ungrouped.

Zero columns

A selection that keeps no column (select(df, -everything())) gives a zero-column table that still knows its row count. A lazy table with pending operations is computed first to get that count.

Performance

Select operations involve copying column data to a new table structure. For very wide tables, selecting fewer columns can significantly reduce memory usage and improve performance of subsequent operations.

See also

filter.tbl_gpu for filtering rows, mutate.tbl_gpu for creating columns, collect.tbl_gpu for retrieving results

Examples

library(dplyr)
if (has_gpu()) {
  gpu_mtcars <- tbl_gpu(mtcars)

  # Select specific columns
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    select(mpg, cyl, hp) |>
    collect()

  # Select with tidyselect helpers
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    select(starts_with("d")) |>
    collect()

  # Reorder columns
  result <- gpu_mtcars |>
    select(hp, mpg, wt) |>
    collect()
}
